frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access or dumping (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SECURITY hive or NTDS.dit extraction, credential-store or DPAPI access, Kerberoasting/AS-REP roasting, or suspicious access to lsass.exe by non-standard processes.

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Credential-access tooling confirmed on scranton: hidden PowerShell stego/IEX loader (PID 2976, parent control.exe) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF, alongside SysinternalsSuite deployment, discovery, keystroke/screenshot jobs and exfil staging.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: LSASS memory access with full-access masks: PowerShell.exe 0x1FFFFF on scranton (03:05:16) and wsmprovhost.exe 0x1F3FFF on nashua (03:09:29); remaining 300+ lsass accesses are svchost/Azure-agent 0x1000/0x1400 and process-start behaviour.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No reg save of SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY, no 4663 access to SAM/SECURITY hives, no hive-export script blocks.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/ntds.dit command lines, file writes or object access; hosts are not domain controllers.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: Only Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC 4662 reads by LOCAL SERVICE (machine account), no lsadump/secretsdump activity.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No SECURITY\Cache object access and no cache/dcc/secretsdump script blocks.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Single 4662 replication-GUID access on newyork by the machine account NEWYORK$ with no DRSUAPI traffic or DCSync tooling; assessed benign.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes' / 'trace stop' on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned by the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) as SYSTEM using the signed Microsoft netsh.exe — legitimate platform diagnostics. No third-party sniffers (pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap/dumpcap/wireshark/tshark), no Npcap/WinPcap driver image loads, no capture-driver service installs, and no capture-related traffic in the zeek window.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input capture toolkit executed on scranton: Get-Keystrokes keylogger job and Invoke-ScreenCapture.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Get-Keystrokes job run at 03:06:59, output viewed at 03:07:36 and job removed at 03:07:49 on scranton.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture function (CopyFromScreen loop, 300s interval, .bmp to Downloads) defined in psversion.ps1 and invoked by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No wwwroot/inetpub/.aspx access, no login-portal file creation, no login/auth/signin HTTP URLs; 'login' hits were file-archive staging scripts.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe (scranton) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua) opened lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF and UNKNOWN call-trace frames; remaining lsass access is benign OS/Azure perf-counter reads.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4771 failures; the only 4776 is a successful validation (Error Code 0x0) for pbeesly. No repeated authentication attempts on any host.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no net user/net use enumeration; PowerShell password matches are module manifests/resource strings.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No hive/NTDS/SAM dump commands or file access; lsass access is dominated by svchost/Azure agents and the 2 PowerShell accesses indicate credential theft (T1003), not cracking.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No spray pattern; 4648 events are UMFD/DWM/machine-account logons and the single runas is a local UAC elevation by pbeesly.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No authentication attempts across multiple accounts; hardcoded credentials in scranton PowerShell scripts relate to certificate export and WebDAV exfiltration, not stuffing.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card interception artifacts: zero process creations with smart-card/credential-provider/MFA command lines in sysmon (event.code:1) and security (4688); no SCardSvr or credential-provider service/DLL installation. The only SmartCard/Credential registry writes are services.exe MuiCache entries and the built-in CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, plus lsass.exe boot-time LSA/CredentialGuard values on scranton. The 4648 explicit-credential events are pbeesly PsExec logons to NASHUA (PSEXESVC), and the 'Credential'-matching script block is an exfiltration function with a hardcoded account password — neither is MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication artifacts in the retrieved data. The only .lnk files are Explorer Recent items and a StartUp persistence shortcut (hostui.lnk) written by the compromised PowerShell process; all 66 outbound SMB connections are System-process traffic to internal hosts 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429; 5140/5145 share access is domain machine-account SYSVOL/IPC$ plus pbeesly ADMIN$ writes for lateral movement; the sole NTLM reference is a once-per-boot LsaSrv 6038 warning; the only WebDAV usage is the attacker's own Invoke-Exfil script mapping \\192.168.0.4\webdav with hardcoded credentials to copy out an archive (exfiltration, not credential coercion). Zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap and shows only internal SMB file access and no WebDAV/PROPFIND HTTP.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: No exploit of a vulnerable service or memory-corruption payload was observed, but the compromised pbeesly PowerShell session (hidden, -ep bypass, launched from control.exe) opened lsass.exe with full-access masks 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton (sysmon EID 10 and security 4656) and wsmprovhost.exe did the same on nashua, alongside LSA registry reads and private-key/clipboard collection. No lsass dump file or MiniDump tooling was found, so credential access via exploitation is suspected but not confirmed.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No access to or copying of browser cookie/credential stores: sysmon code 10 hits on browser images = 0, sysmon code 2 hits = 0, security 4663/4656 object names matching cookie/Login Data/Web Data = 0. The only cookie-related artifacts are a service-profile INetCookies file created by svchost.exe on scranton and rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie WebDAV credential caching for the 192.168.0.4/webdav exfil share; PowerShell 4104 'Cookies/sqlite' hits are Microsoft module manifests and the screen-capture/exfil tooling, not cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credentials harvested: cleartext domain password in PsExec command lines and credential-keyword file collection into working.zip on nashua.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Cleartext dmevals\pbeesly password on PsExec64 command lines and PowerShell script blocks; recursive collection of *pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn files into working.zip.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All credential-named registry writes are OS service/identity/winlogon activity; no hive dumping or stored-credential reads.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history, PSReadLine or Get-History access in sysmon, powershell or security data.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates to .pfx with hardcoded password 'saribas' from the attacker-staged readme.ps1 in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL reads are machine-account GPO refresh (gpt.ini/GptTmpl.inf); no Groups.xml or cpassword access.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Get-Clipboard harvesting and Invoke-Exfil staging of collected credential artifacts on scranton; no direct credential-store file reads observed.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: Clipboard contents read via Get-Clipboard at 03:06:42 on scranton, a common source of pasted credentials; no browser credential database access observed.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No cmdkey/credman/vault execution, no Vault/Credentials registry or file access; only a Credential Guard configuration status message.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden process, file, memory or script activity; observed archiving is bulk file collection for exfiltration.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Attacker-controlled hidden PowerShell (PID 2976, pbeesly, scranton) opened lsass with 0x1FFFFF and wsmprovhost on nashua with 0x1F3FFF, but no authentication-process modification was observed — the access is credential dumping.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: No LSA registry writes, no unexpected lsass module loads, no DC authentication patching; anomalous lsass handles are dump-style access.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages registry change, no DLL dropped to System32, no password-filter references in PowerShell or windows.other.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events and no Reversible/UserAccountControl registry or command-line activity.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136 authentication policy changes; zeek kerberos records show only routine client-to-DC authentication.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory changes and no ADFS/Azure AD Connect or cloud-sync binaries loaded.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider registry writes, DLL loads or file drops; lsass handles reflect memory access, not a registered provider.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No interception/relay evidence in sysmon, security or Zeek data. Outbound connections go to expected internal peers and Microsoft/Azure endpoints. The malicious PsExec+sdelete chain found on scranton/nashua is lateral movement and anti-forensics, not AiTM.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB 445 and NBT-NS 137 traffic is ordinary domain traffic to 10.0.0.4; DNS queries are routine; no DNSClient registry tampering (C232 zero hits); the only NTLM network logon (172.18.39.2) is followed by type 10 logons from the same address, indicating a remote interactive session rather than a relay.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Zeek L2 mapping is stable and one-to-one (10.0.1.6 -> 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 10.0.1.4 -> 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, responder 12:34:56:78:9a:bc consistent); no duplicate MAC for multiple IPs. arp.exe /a, route.exe print and ipconfig /all are read-only diagnostics spawned by Azure Guest Agent/Telemetry/WaAppAgent.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: DHCP-related event codes 1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits and no PowerShell referenced dhcp/netsh. The NDIS Capture start-type changes on scranton are part of an Azure Network Watcher netsh trace packet capture, not DHCP spoofing.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton (0x1F3FFF then 0x1FFFFF) and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (0x1F3FFF) opened lsass.exe with full-access masks alongside a hands-on-keyboard PowerShell toolkit (keystroke logging, screen capture, exfil), indicating credential access — but no Kerberos ticket theft, ticket-dumping tooling or Kerberos anomalies were observed.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No krbtgt dumping, no 'golden'/'krbtgt'/'mimikatz' script blocks, no kdc service installs; 4768/4769 for pbeesly and machine accounts only, AES 0x12, status 0x0.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: No silver-ticket tooling or service-ticket forgery evidence; 4769 service tickets only for machine accounts/krbtgt with AES 0x12 and status 0x0.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No Kerberoast/SPN/GetUserSPNs/Rubeus artifacts; all 4769 tickets use AES 0x12 (no RC4 0x17) and target only machine accounts; Zeek kerberos shows normal single-client AS/TGS flow.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No AS-REP/GetNPUsers/Rubeus artifacts; all 4768 events have PreAuthType 2 with status 0x0, and Zeek AS requests are a normal pbeesly logon with one KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: User-launched PowerShell (PID 2976) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16Z immediately after exporting machine certificates; other high-access lsass events are from OS processes (wininit, csrss, svchost).

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: No cookie-store access or cookie-related script blocks; the single INetCookies file creation is a normal LocalService AppContainer artefact created by svchost.exe.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Get-PrivateKeys in readme.ps1 exported every cert:\LocalMachine certificate to a .pfx with hardcoded password 'saribas' on scranton, producing C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx — private-key theft enabling token forgery.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 5 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a staged script (readme.txt renamed to readme.ps1 and dot-sourced) defining Get-PrivateKeys, which exported every cert:\LocalMachine certificate with Export-PfxCertificate to a randomly named .pfx in Downloads protected by hardcoded password 'saribas'; Sysmon confirmed creation of C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe. Certificate/private-key theft for later authentication abuse.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe PID 2976 — spawned at 02:58:44 by control.exe with a hidden-window, execution-policy-bypass command that decodes a bitmap (C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png) and IEXes the extracted payload — opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 736) at 03:05:16 with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and then 0x1FFFFF, the classic LSASS read-memory mask used by credential dumpers. The call trace ends in UNKNOWN modules, not a signed Windows DLL. The same session had just deployed SysinternalsSuite, run discovery, and later ran keystroke/screenshot jobs, so this is attacker tooling, not administration. A security 4663 event at 03:05:16 records the same powershell.exe (user pbeesly) accessing \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe.
findings.title: PowerShell (steganography/IEX loader) opened LSASS with full-access 0x1FFFFF on scranton

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's PowerShell (running the attacker toolkit loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) invoked Get-Keystrokes at 03:06:59, slept 15 seconds, viewed the 'Keystrokes' job output at 03:07:36 and removed the job at 03:07:49. A Keystroke-Check function enumerating AV products was also defined/run at 03:06:47. This keyboard input capture is new compared with the anchors (which covered screen capture and LSASS access).

PowerShell screen-capture (GUI input capture) script executed on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 03:05:53Z (host scranton.dmevals.local, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, PowerShell PID 3852) a script block defining 'function Invoke-ScreenCapture' was logged (4104). The function starts a background job named "Screenshot" that loops forever, using System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing to grab the full virtual screen via CopyFromScreen and save it as a randomly named .bmp in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads every 300 seconds. It was immediately invoked by a second script block 'Invoke-ScreenCapture;Start-Sleep -Seconds 3;View-Job -JobName "Screenshot"'. The defining script block's Path is C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1, i.e. attacker code appended to a legitimate Sysinternals script. Repeated screen capture of the interactive desktop is GUI input capture used to harvest on-screen credentials/activity.

findings.title: PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with full access (0x1FFFFF / 0x1F3FFF) on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: Sysmon EventID 10 shows C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opening lsass.exe (PID 736) on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02 03:05:16Z with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and, 31 ms earlier, 0x1F3FFF. Both masks include PROCESS_VM_READ/PROCESS_VM_WRITE and full handle rights, and the call trace ends in UNKNOWN modules rather than a signed system DLL — the classic signature of a script/tool reading and manipulating lsass memory (credential API hooking / in-memory credential theft). This is the only non-system process on the estate granted full access to lsass; all other lsass accessors are svchost.exe, Azure telemetry/antimalware perf-counter readers (0x1400), or OS init processes. It occurs ~37 seconds before the Invoke-ScreenCapture script block was logged on the same host, consistent with a single credential-access toolchain.

On scranton.dmevals.local, the PowerShell.exe process (PID 2976, user pbeesly) launched at 02:58:44Z from control.exe with the hidden/encoded command line "PowerShell.exe" -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden -c "sal a New-Object;Add-Type -AssemblyName 'System.Drawing'; ... IEX(...)" opened lsass.exe (PID 736) at 03:05:16Z with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), with an UNKNOWN call-trace frame. Windows security logged the same handle requests (4656, AccessMask 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff, SubjectUserName pbeesly, ProcessName powershell.exe). At 03:09:29Z on nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, remote PowerShell session) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1f3fff, and security 4656 shows SubjectUserName pbeesly. In the same session pbeesly repeatedly opened \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa on nashua (4656/4663, 0x20019/0x1). The same pbeesly PowerShell session on scranton ran credential-adjacent collection: Get-PrivateKeys (exporting cert:\LocalMachine private keys to .pfx with password 'saribas'), Get-Clipboard, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture and Invoke-Exfil. No MiniDump/lsass dump file or dump-writing tool was observed (windows.other lsass/MiniDump query returned 0 hits; only lsass.exe itself matched a *dump* command-line search), so the full-access lsass handles are the strongest exploitation-for-credential-access signal rather than a confirmed dump. Other lsass access in the window is benign: svchost.exe (lsm.dll/sysmain.dll call traces, 0x1000/0x101001/0x3000), wininit.exe/csrss.exe at boot (0x1fffff/0x1000000), and CollectGuestLogs.exe/AntimalwareConfig.exe/WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (0x1410/0x1000).

Surrounding activity (sdelete64 wiping files, accesschk, WebDAV cookie setup to 192.168.0.4, python.exe pushed to NASHUA) confirms a hands-on-keyboard intrusion rather than administrative tooling.

On scranton.dmevals.local, explorer.exe launched C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr with /S at 02:55:56; that process wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png at 02:57:00, the image later decoded by the PowerShell steganography/IEX loader. This is the initial payload delivery that precedes the anchored credential access.

Credential-bearing script blocks and cleartext credentials in files/command lines on SCRANTON

Get-PrivateKeys PowerShell function exported all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files in Downloads
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user pbeesly (SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107), a PowerShell script block named 'Get-PrivateKeys' (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerated cert:\LocalMachine recursively and called Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing each to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected with the hardcoded password 'saribas'. Sysmon recorded the resulting file creation C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe (PID 3876) at 2020-05-02T03:04:57Z, one second after the script block was logged. This is private-key/certificate harvesting for later authentication abuse, part of a broader hands-on-keyboard intrusion on SCRANTON (discovery, Invoke-Exfil to WebDAV 192.168.0.4, PsExec to NASHUA with cleartext credentials).

On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's PowerShell downloaded/extracted SysinternalsSuite.zip, moved it to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, renamed readme.txt to readme.ps1 and dot-sourced it at 03:03:57, then ran Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence and Get-PrivateKeys from it. The Get-PrivateKeys script block records Path: C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1, confirming the certificate-export function came from this attacker-staged script rather than an interactive one-liner. This staging detail is new relative to the anchors.
findings.title: Attacker toolkit (readme.ps1) staged in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite and executed via dot-sourcing on SCRANTON
Credential access from lsass by attacker-controlled PowerShell on SCRANTON, but no authentication-process modification observed
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, parent control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter) was launched with a steganographic payload that decodes bytes from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX's them. At 03:05:16Z that same PID 2976 opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (full access, call trace ending in UNKNOWN module) — classic credential-dump access. The same session ran Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-ScreenCapture and Invoke-SeaDukeStage, and moved laterally to NASHUA (wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720 also opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF; PSEXESVC.exe logons as pbeesly). However, no evidence of authentication-process modification was found: no 4657 writes to LSA/Notification Packages/Reversible-Encryption keys, no 4739/5136 policy changes, no rogue DLLs in System32, and the only LSA registry writes seen are lsass.exe's own ProductType/LsaCfgFlagsDefault values. The lsass access is credential theft (T1003.001 territory), not T1556.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell toolkit disguised as 'readme.ps1' (moved from readme.txt inside a downloaded SysinternalsSuite archive, then dot-sourced with '. .\readme.ps1'). At 2020-05-02T03:04:56Z the script block 'Get-PrivateKeys' was created: it enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. One second later (03:04:57.460Z) Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe (PID 3876). Exporting machine private keys is the prerequisite for forging signed tokens (e.g. SAML assertions) and is not normal user behaviour; the same session also ran Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, accesschk.exe and sdelete64.exe against the dropped payload and archive. The same PowerShell session (PID 2976) also opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16Z.
findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates (private keys) to .pfx with hardcoded password on scranton

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user pbeesly, a script block named Get-PrivateKeys was defined and executed (2020-05-02T03:04:56Z). It enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively, and for every certificate with a thumbprint exports it with Export-PfxCertificate to "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\$RandomFileName.pfx" protected by the hardcoded password "saribas". The script was staged as C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 (preceded by 'Move-Item .\readme.txt readme.ps1' at 03:03:49Z and dot-sourced with '. .\readme.ps1' at 03:03:57Z), i.e. a text file renamed to a script and executed. One second later Sysmon recorded the resulting file creation C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe (PID 3876), confirming the export actually succeeded. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys for later use (e.g. certificate-based authentication / forging). The same host also shows a suspicious binary C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr making outbound connections to 192.168.0.5 shortly before, consistent with an initial-access/execution stage on the same host.

findings.summary: The only packet-capture activity in the Windows window is two netsh.exe executions on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z and 03:19:24Z: 'netsh.exe trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' followed by 'netsh.exe trace stop'. This is the Azure Network Watcher platform agent performing its own diagnostic capture, so it is benign platform behaviour rather than an attacker sniffing credentials. No third-party capture tooling was observed anywhere: zero hits for pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap/dumpcap/wireshark/tshark/npcap/winpcap/promiscuous in sysmon EID 1, security 4688 or PowerShell 4104, and zero sysmon EID 7 image loads matching pcap/npf/wpcap/Packet (no Npcap/WinPcap driver). The 5 EID 7045 service installs are a Java VM support service and four PSEXESVC installs by pbeesly on nashua.dmevals.local (PsExec lateral movement), none of which is a capture driver. The non-overlapping zeek window (2020-04-30) shows only ssl/dns/kerberos/dce_rpc/smb/http services with no capture-related traffic.

No keylogging was observed; the input capture on this estate was screen-based (T1056.002).

Registry write to LocalMachine ROOT certificate store on NASHUA (single event, no certificate content change)
findings.summary: One 4657 registry-modification event on nashua.dmevals.local (2020-05-01T23:16:19Z, subject NASHUA$) touched \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656, but the recorded operation is a value/permission-type change (OperationType %%1905, NewValue and OldValue both %%1800 — unchanged) performed by C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe, i.e. no certificate blob was added or replaced. All other 4657 hits in the window are WMI Autologger EventLog-Application GUID keys, unrelated to certificates. No certificate export, import, or forged-certificate use was observed on NASHUA, so this is not evidence of certificate theft/forgery.

findings.title: Kerberos TGT requests for pbeesly and SCRANTON$ show no certificate-based (PKINIT) pre-authentication
findings.summary: All 14 4768 events in the window are on newyork.dmevals.local: 9 for pbeesly and 5 for the machine account SCRANTON$, all with PreAuthType 2 (encrypted timestamp, i.e. password-based) and Status 0x0. None used PKINIT/certificate pre-authentication, so there is no observed use of a stolen or forged certificate for authentication in this dataset. (The pbeesly TGTs from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 are consistent with normal logons and do not by themselves show certificate abuse.)

incidents.title: PowerShell steganography loader opens LSASS with full-access masks on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same event: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe PID 736 at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF, call trace ending in UNKNOWN modules. This is LSASS memory access consistent with credential dumping (T1003.001). F36/F47/F53 add context (no auth-process modification, no Kerberos theft, preceded by cert export) but center on the same LSASS handle events.

incidents.title: wsmprovhost.exe PowerShell remoting session opens LSASS with 0x1F3FFF on nashua
incidents.rationale: Both describe the same event: wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720 on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe PID 728 at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF via a PowerShell cmdlet call trace. LSASS access from a remoting host is best mapped to T1003.001, though confidence is medium given the Get-Process cmdlet context.

incidents.title: Get-Keystrokes keylogger job on scranton
incidents.rationale: Get-Keystrokes job invoked, viewed and removed in pbeesly's PowerShell is keyboard input capture, matching T1056.001.

incidents.title: PowerShell screen-capture (GUI input capture) on scranton
incidents.rationale: Invoke-ScreenCapture function looping CopyFromScreen to save .bmp files is GUI input capture, matching T1056.002.

incidents.title: Cleartext credentials in files and command lines on scranton (Invoke-Exfil, PsExec64)
incidents.rationale: These describe credentials embedded in files and command lines: Invoke-Exfil's plaintext cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd!, the OfficeSupplies.7z archive, and PsExec64.exe launched with -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by against \\NASHUA. Credentials in files/command lines map to T1552.001.

incidents.title: PowerShell on nashua collects credential-keyword files into working.zip
incidents.rationale: Recursive ChildItem for *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn and similar files compressed into working.zip is collection of credentials in files, matching T1552.001.

incidents.title: PowerShell credential harvesting and exfil staging (clipboard, archive, cleanup) on scranton
incidents.rationale: Get-Clipboard harvesting followed by Invoke-Exfil staging and Invoke-BeachCleanup deleting collected artifacts; clipboard credential harvesting is best mapped to T1555.003 (credentials from password stores/web browsers context) as the closest in-scope technique.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys certificate export to password-protected .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same action: the attacker-staged readme.ps1 toolkit (renamed from readme.txt and dot-sourced) defined and ran Get-PrivateKeys, exporting every LocalMachine certificate with private keys to .pfx files protected by hardcoded password 'saribas'. Stealing authentication certificates/private keys best fits T1649.

incidents.title: csc.exe runtime compilation of attacker DLLs from PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: Add-Type/csc.exe compiling DLLs in Temp is runtime code compilation for execution, not credential access; best mapped to T1027.004.

incidents.title: Screensaver payload drops steganographic monkey.png on scranton
incidents.rationale: Explorer launching C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr which wrote monkey.png is initial payload delivery/execution, not credential access; best mapped to T1204 (User Execution).

incidents.title: hostui.exe -verb runas elevation and registry-value Invoke-Expression on scranton
incidents.rationale: Start-Process hostui.exe -verb runas followed by registry-value IEX and reflective loader is privilege escalation/execution, best mapped to T1548.002 (Bypass User Account Control).

incidents.title: sdclt.exe UAC-bypass pattern with HKCU Folder shell open command on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe launches with HKCU\Software\Classes\Folder\shell\open\command DelegateExecute manipulation is a UAC bypass, best mapped to T1548.002.
